extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and practitioners of journalism and media studies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and descriptive criteria for the role, functions, historical practices, and public/evaluative perceptions of news presenters (anchors/newscasters) across TV, radio and online news programs. Includes responsibilities, typical working conditions, and common criticisms about credibility and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic definition / function
rubrics_metrics.description: A news presenter – also known as a newsreader, newscaster, anchorman/anchorwoman, news anchor or anchor – is a person who presents news during a news program on TV, radio or the Internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core role: presenting the news to an audience as part of a broadcast or online program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working journalist responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: They may also be a working journalist, assisting in the collection of news material and may, in addition, provide commentary during the program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some presenters are active reporters who gather material themselves and contribute editorially; others primarily present preprepared copy. Capability to assist in news collection and to provide informed commentary is a substantive dimension of the role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work environment and location
rubrics_metrics.description: News presenters most often work from a television studio or radio studio, but may also present the news from remote locations in the field related to a particular major news event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations can consider whether a presenter is effective in-studio versus on-location (field) reporting and whether they can adapt presentation style and technical constraints across settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading and writing news copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Classically, the presenter would read the news from news 'copy' which they may or may not have helped write with a news writer. This was often taken almost directly from wire services and then rewritten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skill in reading prepared copy and in contributing to writing/editing (or working with writers) is a relevant criterion; historical practice emphasized reading wire/rewritten text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviewing and improvised commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchors interview experts about various aspects of breaking news stories, and themselves provided improvised commentary, all under the supervision of the lead (or main) producer, who coordinated the broadcast by communicating with the anchor through an earphone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should consider a presenter's ability to conduct expert interviews, improvise informed commentary in breaking situations, and follow producer direction/technical cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing/editing involvement vs role distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Many anchors help write or edit news for their programs, although modern news formats often distinguish between anchor and commentator in an attempt to establish the 'character' of a news anchor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the presenter contributes to editorial content (writing/editing) or primarily serves a presentational/character role; modern formats may separate these functions deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility and trust-building
rubrics_metrics.description: Some critics defend the role of the anchor in society, claiming that they function as a necessary conduit of credibility. The news anchor's nightly presence as a necessary way to build familiarity and trust between the network and its viewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key evaluative metric is the extent to which the presenter fosters viewer trust and perceived credibility through consistent, reliable presence and authoritative delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of sensationalization / personality overshadowing content
rubrics_metrics.description: Some argue anchors have become sensationalized characters whose identities overshadow the news itself, with 'reading headlines to a camera in an appealing way [being] incentivized over actual reporting'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: prioritizing personality/entertainment value over substantive reporting. Evaluation should flag when an anchor's celebrity or performative style distracts from journalistic content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regurgitation vs original reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: A criticism levied against the role is that anchors simply 'regurgitat[e] or reproduc[e] the report of others', differentiating them from the productive occupations of journalists and on-site reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure whether a presenter adds unique reporting, analysis, or oversight versus merely relaying others' reports; originality and editorial contribution are quality indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic/authority role and social responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The anchor represents a 'symbolic representation of the institutional order as an integrated totality' and functions similarly to other authority-bearing public personas; responsibility for interpreting the world and posing a political course of action and a social agenda may fall on such public personas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the ethical and societal influence of anchors: their role as perceived authorities creates responsibilities (e.g., avoiding bottlenecking of information, balancing interpretation and impartiality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choreography, performativity, and audience engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: The choreography and performativity involved in the construction of the news broadcast dramatizes political processes, but in doing so, exposes its flattening of subjectivity and insistence upon itself as the final word of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a presenter's performative skills (delivery, pacing, stagecraft) for audience engagement, while also assessing whether performativity compromises journalistic depth or democratic participation.
